what_it_does: Running a large language model (LLM) row by row over a database table — to classify, summarise, or extract information from each record — is enormously slow and expensive because the model keeps re-reading the same repeated context from scratch. This paper shows that simply reordering the rows (and the fields within each row) before sending them to the model can dramatically increase how often the model's internal memory (the key-value cache) already contains the shared prefix, cutting query time by up to 3.4x and API costs by up to 32%.
method_in_detail:
The idea. When a language model processes a prompt, it builds an internal state for every token (the key-value cache, or KV cache). If the next prompt starts with the same words as the previous one, the model can skip re-reading that shared prefix — this is called a cache hit. Tables are full of repeated values: the same product title across many reviews, the same column headings, the same background context for a RAG query. Sending rows in their default order wastes those repeated prefixes. The goal is to find an ordering that maximises the total number of shared-prefix tokens (the prefix hit count, PHC) across all rows.

Why field order matters too. If a column containing unique IDs appears first in every row, there is never a shared prefix. Moving shared-value columns to the front — and doing this differently for each row based on what that row's values actually are — can multiply the hit count by as much as the number of fields.

Optimal algorithm (OPHR). For a table with n rows and m fields, the optimal algorithm (called Optimal Prefix Hit Recursion) recursively partitions the table: pick a field and a specific value, put all rows sharing that value into one group, recurse on both parts, combine. This is provably optimal but has exponential worst-case runtime — impractical for tables with thousands of rows.

Greedy algorithm (GGR). The practical algorithm (Greedy Group Recursion) does the same recursive split but at each step only picks the single field-value combination with the highest estimated hit count, rather than trying all of them. Two additional accelerations make it fast: (1) functional dependencies — if knowing a product ID uniquely determines the product title, there is no need to consider the title as an independent split; (2) early stopping based on cardinality and average value length statistics, avoiding scans of large subtables. GGR runs in under 15 seconds even for tables with 30,000 rows and 57 fields.

The key design choice. Per-row field reordering rather than a single fixed field order for all rows. A fixed order can be up to m times worse than per-row reordering in the worst case, because different rows benefit from leading with different shared values.

The result. On 16 benchmark queries using Llama-3-8B and Llama-3-70B, GGR achieves 1.5-3.4x speedup over naive caching with the default row/field order, and 1.8-3.8x over no caching at all. Cache hit rates jump from 10-50% to 57-86% across datasets. On OpenAI and Anthropic API pricing (which discount cached tokens), this translates to 20-39% cost savings, up to 32% measured directly on the API.
what_it_does_plain: This paper shows that the order in which you feed database rows to an AI model — and the order of fields within each row — has a huge effect on cost and speed, because models can reuse computation for identical prefixes. A fast greedy reordering algorithm (GGR) finds a near-optimal order in seconds and delivers up to 3.4x faster queries and 32% lower API bills with no change to the answers.
